title: 1933 Imperial Airways Diksmuide crash
summary: On 28 March 1933, an Armstrong Whitworth Argosy II named City of Liverpool crashed near Diksmuide, Belgium, killing all 15 people aboard. The aircraft caught fire while flying over Belgium, with fire originating toward the rear of the plane. A passenger was seen exiting the aircraft without a parachute. Investigators concluded the fire resulted from combustible substance fired either accidentally or deliberately, possibly a deliberate act of sabotage.
probable_cause: Fire started toward the rear of the plane in either the lavatory or luggage area from combustible substance. Possible deliberate sabotage by passenger Albert Voss involving flammable substances accessible to him.

factors.evidence: The plane was seen to catch fire while flying over fields of northern Belgium.
It has been suggested this was the first airliner ever lost to sabotage, with suspicion centered on one passenger, Albert Voss, who was seen exiting the aircraft before impact.
No items recovered from the front portion of the wreckage showed evidence of fire damage before impact, nor was there evidence in the engines or fuel systems, suggesting rear location access.
The aircraft split into two sections at approximately 200 feet and hit the ground separately, instantly killing all those still on board.

events.text: Aircraft caught fire while flying over fields of northern Belgium.
A passenger was seen to exit the aircraft and fall to earth without a parachute at approximately 200 feet altitude.
Aircraft split into two sections at approximately 200 feet and hit the ground separately, killing all on board.
Fire had started towards the rear of the plane in either the lavatory or the luggage area at the back of the cabin.

notes: Cause uncertain; investigators concluded fire origin ambiguous between accident and deliberate act

title: 1933 Tupolev ANT-7 Podolsk crash
summary: A Soviet aviation disaster occurred on September 5, 1933, resulting in eight fatalities. Limited information exists about the cause or circumstances of this accident.

events.text: Soviet aviation disaster with eight fatalities

title: 1933 United Airlines Boeing 247 mid-air explosion
summary: A Boeing 247 exploded and crashed near Chesterton, Indiana on October 10, 1933. The aircraft was carrying 3 crew and 4 passengers en route from Cleveland to Chicago when an explosive device detonated in the baggage compartment, fragmenting the structure and severing the tail section just aft of the toilet. The aircraft descended in flames and impacted a wooded area, with a secondary explosion occurring after impact. Investigators determined nitroglycerin was the probable explosive, though no suspect was identified.
probable_cause: On-board explosive device (bomb) in the baggage compartment.

factors.evidence: Explosive device detonated in baggage compartment; metal fragments riddled inside of toilet door and shards found wedged from impact.
Explosive device caused rapid explosive decompression through baggage compartment and fuselage breaching.
Tail section severed just aft of the toilet and found mostly intact nearly 1 mile away from main wreckage.
Second explosion followed after the aircraft crashed into the wooded area.

Aircraft impacted wooded Jackson Township farm 5 miles outside Chesterton
Second explosion followed after aircraft crashed

title: 1933 Imperial Airways Ruysselede crash
summary: An Avro Ten operated by Imperial Airways collided with a guy wire of an 870 ft tall radio mast at Ruysselede, Belgium on 30 December 1933 whilst flying at an altitude of 250 ft in fog. The aircraft lost a wing and crashed, killing all ten passengers and crew.
probable_cause: The aircraft descended to unsafe altitude in fog, causing collision with radio mast guy wire. Flying on a route to the north of its normal route due to fog contributed to the navigation error.

factors.evidence: as a result of fog, the aircraft was flying on a route to the north of its normal route
flying on a route to the north of its normal route
whilst flying at an altitude of 250 ft
it crashed into a guy wire of the 870 ft tall radio mast at Ruysselede
The Avro Ten registration G-ABLU lost a wing after striking the radio mast at Ruysselede at 250 feet altitude, witnessed by workers at the radio station and villagers from Ruysselede.
There was an explosion and the wreckage of the aircraft was burnt out.

events.text: Aircraft departed 20 minutes later than scheduled at 12:20 local time.
At 13:15, whilst flying at an altitude of 250 ft, it crashed into a guy wire of the 870 ft tall radio mast at Ruysselede.
The top section of the mast was demolished and the aircraft was damaged in the impact.
There was an explosion and the wreckage of the aircraft was burnt out.
